headline: Terns Are Working Great Point Like They Know Something We Don't
subhead: No green flashes on the Shoals yet, but the bird sign, the bait, and the water temps say bonito are close — meanwhile the stripers and blues are already paying rent in the rips.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, first light, I'm sitting on the west side of the Great Point rip watching a mixed flock of terns work a nervous patch of water about eighty yards off the bar. They're diving hard, dropping and lifting, the way they do when there's something small and fast pushing bait up from underneath. I watched that spot for twenty minutes waiting for a green flash to break the surface — that first bonito of the year cutting through a peanut school — and it never came. What did come was a bluefish blowup, chunky three-to-five pound cocktail blues absolutely wrecking the same bait, which is its own kind of good news, just not the news I was hoping to write about this week.

Here's where we're at. The bonito aren't here yet on Nantucket Shoals, but I don't think it's a long wait. The signs pointing that direction out of Rhode Island breachways and the Vineyard rips earlier this week are exactly the kind of leading edge that tends to show up on our side of the Sound within days, not weeks — that's the sequence I've watched play out for going on fifteen years, RI and the Vineyard first, then Nantucket Shoals and Great Point catch the spillover. If that pattern holds, and there's no reason yet to think it won't with this stable weather sitting over us, I'd expect the first confirmed bonito over the Shoals sometime in the next week to ten days. Albies are behind that again — Great Point doesn't usually see its first real showing until deeper into August, so don't burn your legs off chasing false albacore just yet. Chase the terns instead and see what's actually under them.

What's real and biting right now is the striper work in the rips, and it's a nighttime and low-light game almost exclusively. Surface water in the Sound has settled into that classic mid-summer pattern — warm enough on top that the bigger fish have slid down onto structure and pushed their feeding into the dark hours and the tide changes. I've had my best luck working the drop on the north side of Old Man Shoal on the last two hours of the ebb, eels drifted just off bottom in eighteen to twenty-five feet, letting the current do the work instead of working the rod. Bass Rip has been doing the same thing — quiet at midday, then turning on hard about an hour before dark as the current builds and bait gets pinned against the shoal edge. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, weight enough to hold bottom in that current, have out-produced eels for some boats this week, especially on the tail end of the tide when the current slackens just enough for the chunks to sit still.

Fluke have pushed off the shallow flats entirely — too warm up top — and settled onto the deeper structure where the bottom stays workable. Monomoy Channel and the edges of Stone Horse Shoal have been the most consistent producers, twenty-two to thirty-two feet, drifting bucktail and Gulp combinations, four-inch white or chartreuse swimming mullets on three-quarter-ounce heads, dragged slow and heavy on the bottom of the drift. Nothing spectacular size-wise — most of what's coming over the rail is fifteen to eighteen inches with the occasional keeper mixed in — but it's steady enough that a couple hours over that structure on a moving tide will put fish in the box.

The bluefish have been the most dependable thing going, and that lines up with what we flagged a few days back about cocktail blues tracking the peanut bunker as it spreads through the back-bay and inlet zones — that's exactly what's happening off Monomoy and around the Chatham break right now, tighter schools of smaller blues chopping through bait pods in six to fifteen feet, easy pickings on top-water poppers or small metal if you can find the surface activity before it moves. The adult blues, the four-to-eight pound class, are running with bigger bunker schools out in open water off Great Point and Horseshoe Shoal, and those fish will hit bigger swimming plugs or bunker spoons trolled just outside the structure.

Tide and moon-wise, we're building out of the recent slack period toward fuller tides again, which should sharpen up the current-dependent spots — the Handkerchief, Bass Rip, the Monomoy rips on the outgoing — over the next several days. Stronger current means tighter bait concentrations, which means better odds on everything from the stripers to whatever shows up first when the bonito finally arrive.

Looking ahead, if the calm weather holds — and right now there's nothing on the radar to say it won't — I'd put my money on Nantucket Shoals and Great Point producing the first confirmed bonito of the season sometime in the next week to ten days, riding the same warm push that's already the Vineyard and RI side. Until then, work the low-light stripers on the shoal edges, hit the fluke grounds off Monomoy on a moving tide, and keep an eye on the birds. They usually know before we do.
